games.title: Name the type
games.instructions: Match each expression to the type Python gives it.

pairs.explanation: A whole number with no decimal point is an int.
A decimal point makes it a float.
Quotes make it a string, even when it looks like a number.
Square brackets make a list.
The trailing comma is what makes (7,) a tuple; (7) is just 7.
True and False are the two bool values.

games.title: Can it change?
games.instructions: Sort each value by whether it can be changed in place.

items.explanation: Lists are mutable: nums[0] = 9 works.
Dictionaries are mutable: you can add and replace keys.
Sets are mutable: add() and remove() change them.
Strings are immutable: name[5] = 'X' raises a TypeError.
Tuples are immutable once made.
Numbers are immutable; x = x + 1 makes a new number.

games.title: Sort by type
games.instructions: Put each expression under the type of value it produces.

items.explanation: // on two ints gives an int: 3.
len always returns an int.

games.title: Error or fine?
games.instructions: Sort each line by whether it runs or raises an error.

items.explanation: index raises ValueError when the item is not in the list.
A missing key raises KeyError.
int only reads digits: ValueError.

Tuples cannot be changed: TypeError.

games.title: Dictionaries and scope
games.instructions: Find each piece of code and what it prints.

pairs.explanation: len counts the keys.
get returns the default when the key is missing.
keys() gives the keys in the order they were added.
104 and 105 are the character codes for h and i.

pairs.a:
counter = 1
def add():
    global counter
    counter += 3
add()
print(counter)
pairs.explanation: global lets the function change the outer counter.
join puts the string between each item.
